children.proof_nl:
Because 0 <= a <= b and r >= 0, the integers a, b, r+a, and r+b are all nonnegative, so every q-Pochhammer symbol appearing in the claimed identity is defined.

First consider the case a = b. By the definition of P_{a,b,r}(q), the product from i = a+1 to b is empty, so P_{a,b,r}(q) = 1. On the other hand,
((q;q)_{r+b} (q;q)_a) / ((q;q)_{r+a} (q;q)_b)
= ((q;q)_{r+a} (q;q)_a) / ((q;q)_{r+a} (q;q)_a)
= 1.
So the identity holds when a = b.

Now assume a < b. We use the following elementary consequence of the definition of (q;q)_n: for any nonnegative integers m < n,
(q;q)_n = (q;q)_m \prod_{j=m+1}^n (1 - q^j).
Indeed, if m = 0 then this is just (q;q)_n = 1 \cdot \prod_{j=1}^n (1 - q^j), using (q;q)_0 = 1; if m > 0, it follows by splitting the defining product for (q;q)_n after the factor j = m.

Apply this with m = r+a and n = r+b. Since a < b, we have r+a < r+b, so
(q;q)_{r+b} = (q;q)_{r+a} \prod_{j=r+a+1}^{r+b} (1 - q^j).
Apply it again with m = a and n = b:
(q;q)_b = (q;q)_a \prod_{j=a+1}^{b} (1 - q^j).

Since each factor 1 - q^j is a nonzero polynomial, these products are invertible in the rational function field Z(q). Therefore,
((q;q)_{r+b} (q;q)_a) / ((q;q)_{r+a} (q;q)_b)
= \frac{\prod_{j=r+a+1}^{r+b} (1 - q^j)}{\prod_{j=a+1}^{b} (1 - q^j)}.

Now reindex the numerator by writing j = r+i. As j runs from r+a+1 to r+b, the index i runs from a+1 to b. Hence
\prod_{j=r+a+1}^{r+b} (1 - q^j) = \prod_{i=a+1}^{b} (1 - q^{r+i}).
Substituting this gives
((q;q)_{r+b} (q;q)_a) / ((q;q)_{r+a} (q;q)_b)
= \frac{\prod_{i=a+1}^{b} (1 - q^{r+i})}{\prod_{i=a+1}^{b} (1 - q^i)}
= \prod_{i=a+1}^{b} \frac{1 - q^{r+i}}{1 - q^i}
= P_{a,b,r}(q),
where the last equality is exactly the definition of P_{a,b,r}(q).

Thus, in all cases,
P_{a,b,r}(q) = ((q;q)_{r+b} (q;q)_a) / ((q;q)_{r+a} (q;q)_b)
in the rational function field Z(q).

children.proof_nl:
Set e_d := floor((r+b)/d) + floor(a/d) - floor((r+a)/d) - floor(b/d). The hypothesis says that for every positive integer d,
floor((r+b)/d) - floor((r+a)/d) >= floor(b/d) - floor(a/d).
Rearranging gives
 e_d = [floor((r+b)/d) - floor((r+a)/d)] - [floor(b/d) - floor(a/d)] >= 0.
Thus e_d is a nonnegative integer for every positive d, and in particular for every d with 1 <= d <= r+b.

Now rewrite R_{a,b,r}(q). From the definition (q;q)_n = product_{j=1}^n (1-q^j), we have
 (q;q)_{r+b}/(q;q)_{r+a} = product_{m=r+a+1}^{r+b} (1-q^m),
while
 (q;q)_a/(q;q)_b = 1 / product_{j=a+1}^{b} (1-q^j).
Therefore
 R_{a,b,r}(q) = product_{j=a+1}^{b} ((1-q^{r+j})/(1-q^j)),
with the usual empty-product value 1 when a=b.

For each integer m >= 1, use the standard cyclotomic factorization
 q^m - 1 = product_{d|m} Phi_d(q).
Then
 1 - q^m = -(q^m - 1) = - product_{d|m} Phi_d(q).
Hence for each j,
 (1-q^{r+j})/(1-q^j)
 = [ - product_{d|(r+j)} Phi_d(q) ] / [ - product_{d|j} Phi_d(q) ]
 = product_{d|(r+j)} Phi_d(q) * product_{d|j} Phi_d(q)^(-1).
Multiplying these identities over j = a+1, ..., b and collecting equal cyclotomic factors, the exponent of Phi_d(q) in the total product is
 c_d := #{j : a < j <= b, d | (r+j)} - #{j : a < j <= b, d | j}.

The first count is the number of multiples of d in the interval [r+a+1, r+b], so
 #{j : a < j <= b, d | (r+j)} = floor((r+b)/d) - floor((r+a)/d).
The second count is the number of multiples of d in [a+1, b], so
 #{j : a < j <= b, d | j} = floor(b/d) - floor(a/d).
Therefore
 c_d = floor((r+b)/d) + floor(a/d) - floor((r+a)/d) - floor(b/d) = e_d.

If d > r+b, then both counts are 0, because every integer occurring in the two intervals is at most r+b. Hence c_d = 0 for d > r+b. Thus the factorization is finite and equals
 R_{a,b,r}(q) = product_{d=1}^{r+b} Phi_d(q)^(e_d).
This is exactly the asserted cyclotomic factorization.

Finally, each e_d is a nonnegative integer, and each cyclotomic polynomial Phi_d(q) lies in Z[q]. Therefore the finite product product_{d=1}^{r+b} Phi_d(q)^(e_d) belongs to Z[q]. Hence R_{a,b,r}(q) belongs to Z[q].

children.proof_nl:
First note that D = r(b-a) is a nonnegative integer.

If a = b, then
R_{a,b,r}(q) = ((q;q)_{r+a}(q;q)_a)/((q;q)_{r+a}(q;q)_a) = 1,
and D = 0. Hence q^D R_{a,b,r}(q^(-1)) = 1 = R_{a,b,r}(q). If R_{a,b,r}(q) lies in Z[q], we may take c_0 = 1, and the required symmetry is immediate.

It remains to treat the case a < b. From the definition of (q;q)_n,
(q;q)_{r+b} / (q;q)_{r+a} = product_{t=r+a+1}^{r+b} (1 - q^t) = product_{i=a+1}^{b} (1 - q^(r+i)),
and
(q;q)_a / (q;q)_b = 1 / product_{i=a+1}^{b} (1 - q^i).
Therefore
R_{a,b,r}(q) = product_{i=a+1}^{b} ((1 - q^(r+i)) / (1 - q^i)).

Evaluate at q^(-1). For each i,
(1 - q^(-(r+i))) / (1 - q^(-i)) = (-q^(-(r+i))(1 - q^(r+i))) / (-q^(-i)(1 - q^i)) = q^(-r) (1 - q^(r+i)) / (1 - q^i).
Multiplying these identities for i = a+1, ..., b gives
R_{a,b,r}(q^(-1)) = product_{i=a+1}^{b} q^(-r) (1 - q^(r+i)) / (1 - q^i)
= q^(-r(b-a)) product_{i=a+1}^{b} (1 - q^(r+i)) / (1 - q^i)
= q^(-D) R_{a,b,r}(q).
Multiplying by q^D yields the rational-function identity
q^D R_{a,b,r}(q^(-1)) = R_{a,b,r}(q)
in Z(q).

Now assume additionally that R_{a,b,r}(q) belongs to Z[q]. Since each factor 1 - q^m is a nonzero polynomial, the quotient defining R_{a,b,r}(q) is nonzero in Z(q); hence, when it lies in Z[q], it is a nonzero polynomial. Write
R_{a,b,r}(q) = sum_{j=0}^{m} d_j q^j
with d_m != 0 and each d_j in Z.
The self-reciprocity identity gives
sum_{j=0}^{m} d_j q^j = q^D R_{a,b,r}(q^(-1)) = sum_{j=0}^{m} d_j q^(D-j).
If some d_j with j > D were nonzero, then the right-hand side would contain the negative power q^(D-j). These exponents D-j are all distinct, so such a negative-power term could not cancel with any other term. But the left-hand side is an ordinary polynomial and has no negative powers. Therefore d_j = 0 for every j > D, so m <= D.

Now define integers c_0, ..., c_D by c_j = d_j for 0 <= j <= m and c_j = 0 for m < j <= D. Then
R_{a,b,r}(q) = sum_{j=0}^{D} c_j q^j.
Using again q^D R_{a,b,r}(q^(-1)) = R_{a,b,r}(q), we get
sum_{j=0}^{D} c_j q^j = q^D R_{a,b,r}(q^(-1)) = sum_{j=0}^{D} c_j q^(D-j) = sum_{j=0}^{D} c_{D-j} q^j,
where the last equality is the reindexing j -> D-j. Since equal polynomials have equal coefficients, c_j = c_{D-j} for every 0 <= j <= D.

This proves both the rational-function identity and the palindromic coefficient statement.

children.proof_nl:
Let N := r+a+b. Since 0 <= a <= b and r >= 0, we have N >= b >= a >= 0; in particular 0 <= a <= N and 0 <= b <= N, and also N-a = r+b >= 0 and N-b = r+a >= 0. By the standard polynomial form of Gaussian q-binomial coefficients, for 0 <= t <= N one has [N choose t]_q = (q;q)_N / ((q;q)_t (q;q)_{N-t}). Therefore
[N choose b]_q / [N choose a]_q = ((q;q)_N / ((q;q)_b (q;q)_{N-b})) / ((q;q)_N / ((q;q)_a (q;q)_{N-a})) = ((q;q)_a (q;q)_{N-a}) / ((q;q)_b (q;q)_{N-b}).
Using N-a = r+b and N-b = r+a, this becomes
[N choose b]_q / [N choose a]_q = ((q;q)_{r+b} (q;q)_a) / ((q;q)_{r+a} (q;q)_b) = R_{a,b,r}(q).
Thus R_{a,b,r}(q) is exactly a quotient of two Gaussian q-binomial coefficients. By hypothesis R_{a,b,r}(q) belongs to Z[q], so this quotient is a polynomial in q. Applying the allowed semantic anchor with n = N, k = b, and l = a, we conclude that every coefficient of R_{a,b,r}(q) is nonnegative. Since R_{a,b,r}(q) is in Z[q], all of its coefficients are integers. Therefore, for every integer j with 0 <= j <= floor(D/2), the coefficient of q^j in R_{a,b,r}(q) is a nonnegative integer. This proves the lemma.

children.proof_nl:
Let j be any integer with 0 <= j <= D. We will prove that c_j >= 0.

If j <= floor(D/2), then c_j >= 0 by the given hypothesis on the first half of the coefficients.

Now suppose j > floor(D/2). We claim that D - j <= floor(D/2). Indeed, if D - j were also > floor(D/2), then, since j and D-j are integers, we would have j >= floor(D/2) + 1 and D - j >= floor(D/2) + 1. Adding these inequalities gives
D = j + (D-j) >= 2 floor(D/2) + 2.
But 2 floor(D/2) is either D or D-1, so 2 floor(D/2) + 2 > D, a contradiction. Therefore D-j <= floor(D/2). Also D-j >= 0 because j <= D.

Hence 0 <= D-j <= floor(D/2), so by the hypothesis on the first half of the coefficients we get c_{D-j} >= 0. Using the symmetry hypothesis, c_j = c_{D-j}, and therefore c_j >= 0.

Since j was arbitrary, we have proved that c_j >= 0 for every integer j with 0 <= j <= D. Equivalently, every coefficient of F(q) is nonnegative.

Then one has the identity in the rational function field Z(q): P_{a,b,r}(q) = ((q;q)_{r+b} (q;q)_a) / ((q;q)_{r+a} (q;q)_b).
Because 0 <= a <= b and r >= 0, the integers a, b, r+a, and r+b are all nonnegative, so every q-Pochhammer symbol appearing in the claimed identity is defined.

First consider the case a = b. By the definition of P_{a,b,r}(q), the product from i = a+1 to b is empty, so P_{a,b,r}(q) = 1. On the other hand,
((q;q)_{r+b} (q;q)_a) / ((q;q)_{r+a} (q;q)_b)
= ((q;q)_{r+a} (q;q)_a) / ((q;q)_{r+a} (q;q)_a)
= 1.
So the identity holds when a = b.

Now assume a < b. We use the following elementary consequence of the definition of (q;q)_n: for any nonnegative integers m < n,
(q;q)_n = (q;q)_m \prod_{j=m+1}^n (1 - q^j).
Indeed, if m = 0 then this is just (q;q)_n = 1 \cdot \prod_{j=1}^n (1 - q^j), using (q;q)_0 = 1; if m > 0, it follows by splitting the defining product for (q;q)_n after the factor j = m.

Apply this with m = r+a and n = r+b. Since a < b, we have r+a < r+b, so
(q;q)_{r+b} = (q;q)_{r+a} \prod_{j=r+a+1}^{r+b} (1 - q^j).
Apply it again with m = a and n = b:
(q;q)_b = (q;q)_a \prod_{j=a+1}^{b} (1 - q^j).

Since each factor 1 - q^j is a nonzero polynomial, these products are invertible in the rational function field Z(q). Therefore,
((q;q)_{r+b} (q;q)_a) / ((q;q)_{r+a} (q;q)_b)
= \frac{\prod_{j=r+a+1}^{r+b} (1 - q^j)}{\prod_{j=a+1}^{b} (1 - q^j)}.

Now reindex the numerator by writing j = r+i. As j runs from r+a+1 to r+b, the index i runs from a+1 to b. Hence
\prod_{j=r+a+1}^{r+b} (1 - q^j) = \prod_{i=a+1}^{b} (1 - q^{r+i}).
Substituting this gives
((q;q)_{r+b} (q;q)_a) / ((q;q)_{r+a} (q;q)_b)
= \frac{\prod_{i=a+1}^{b} (1 - q^{r+i})}{\prod_{i=a+1}^{b} (1 - q^i)}
= \prod_{i=a+1}^{b} \frac{1 - q^{r+i}}{1 - q^i}
= P_{a,b,r}(q),
where the last equality is exactly the definition of P_{a,b,r}(q).

Thus, in all cases,
P_{a,b,r}(q) = ((q;q)_{r+b} (q;q)_a) / ((q;q)_{r+a} (q;q)_b)
in the rational function field Z(q).

2. lem_20260329092508_dde83cd9: For integers a, b, r with 0 <= a <= b and r >= 0, let q be an indeterminate, define (q;q)_n := product_{j=1}^n (1 - q^j) for n >= 0 with (q;q)_0 := 1, and set R_{a,b,r}(q) := ((q;q)_{r+b} (q;q)_a) / ((q;q)_{r+a} (q;q)_b). Assume that for every positive integer d one has floor((r+b)/d) - floor((r+a)/d) >= floor(b/d) - floor(a/d). Then for every integer d with 1 <= d <= r+b, the integer e_d := floor((r+b)/d) + floor(a/d) - floor((r+a)/d) - floor(b/d) is nonnegative, and one has the cyclotomic factorization R_{a,b,r}(q) = product_{d=1}^{r+b} Phi_d(q)^(e_d), where Phi_d(q) is the d-th cyclotomic polynomial. In particular, R_{a,b,r}(q) belongs to Z[q].
Set e_d := floor((r+b)/d) + floor(a/d) - floor((r+a)/d) - floor(b/d). The hypothesis says that for every positive integer d,
floor((r+b)/d) - floor((r+a)/d) >= floor(b/d) - floor(a/d).
Rearranging gives
 e_d = [floor((r+b)/d) - floor((r+a)/d)] - [floor(b/d) - floor(a/d)] >= 0.
Thus e_d is a nonnegative integer for every positive d, and in particular for every d with 1 <= d <= r+b.

Now rewrite R_{a,b,r}(q). From the definition (q;q)_n = product_{j=1}^n (1-q^j), we have
 (q;q)_{r+b}/(q;q)_{r+a} = product_{m=r+a+1}^{r+b} (1-q^m),
while
 (q;q)_a/(q;q)_b = 1 / product_{j=a+1}^{b} (1-q^j).
Therefore
 R_{a,b,r}(q) = product_{j=a+1}^{b} ((1-q^{r+j})/(1-q^j)),
with the usual empty-product value 1 when a=b.

For each integer m >= 1, use the standard cyclotomic factorization
 q^m - 1 = product_{d|m} Phi_d(q).
Then
 1 - q^m = -(q^m - 1) = - product_{d|m} Phi_d(q).
Hence for each j,
 (1-q^{r+j})/(1-q^j)
 = [ - product_{d|(r+j)} Phi_d(q) ] / [ - product_{d|j} Phi_d(q) ]
 = product_{d|(r+j)} Phi_d(q) * product_{d|j} Phi_d(q)^(-1).
Multiplying these identities over j = a+1, ..., b and collecting equal cyclotomic factors, the exponent of Phi_d(q) in the total product is
 c_d := #{j : a < j <= b, d | (r+j)} - #{j : a < j <= b, d | j}.

The first count is the number of multiples of d in the interval [r+a+1, r+b], so
 #{j : a < j <= b, d | (r+j)} = floor((r+b)/d) - floor((r+a)/d).
The second count is the number of multiples of d in [a+1, b], so
 #{j : a < j <= b, d | j} = floor(b/d) - floor(a/d).
Therefore
 c_d = floor((r+b)/d) + floor(a/d) - floor((r+a)/d) - floor(b/d) = e_d.

If d > r+b, then both counts are 0, because every integer occurring in the two intervals is at most r+b. Hence c_d = 0 for d > r+b. Thus the factorization is finite and equals
 R_{a,b,r}(q) = product_{d=1}^{r+b} Phi_d(q)^(e_d).
This is exactly the asserted cyclotomic factorization.

Finally, each e_d is a nonnegative integer, and each cyclotomic polynomial Phi_d(q) lies in Z[q]. Therefore the finite product product_{d=1}^{r+b} Phi_d(q)^(e_d) belongs to Z[q]. Hence R_{a,b,r}(q) belongs to Z[q].

3. lem_20260329092532_2c3e34d7: For integers a, b, r with 0 <= a <= b and r >= 0, let q be an indeterminate, define (q;q)_n := product_{j=1}^n (1 - q^j) for n >= 0 with (q;q)_0 := 1, set R_{a,b,r}(q) := ((q;q)_{r+b} (q;q)_a) / ((q;q)_{r+a} (q;q)_b), and define D := r (b - a). Then the rational-function identity q^D R_{a,b,r}(q^(-1)) = R_{a,b,r}(q) holds in Z(q). Consequently, whenever R_{a,b,r}(q) belongs to Z[q], there exist integers c_0, ..., c_D such that R_{a,b,r}(q) = sum_{j=0}^D c_j q^j and c_j = c_{D-j} for every j with 0 <= j <= D.
First note that D = r(b-a) is a nonnegative integer.

If a = b, then
R_{a,b,r}(q) = ((q;q)_{r+a}(q;q)_a)/((q;q)_{r+a}(q;q)_a) = 1,
and D = 0. Hence q^D R_{a,b,r}(q^(-1)) = 1 = R_{a,b,r}(q). If R_{a,b,r}(q) lies in Z[q], we may take c_0 = 1, and the required symmetry is immediate.

It remains to treat the case a < b. From the definition of (q;q)_n,
(q;q)_{r+b} / (q;q)_{r+a} = product_{t=r+a+1}^{r+b} (1 - q^t) = product_{i=a+1}^{b} (1 - q^(r+i)),
and
(q;q)_a / (q;q)_b = 1 / product_{i=a+1}^{b} (1 - q^i).
Therefore
R_{a,b,r}(q) = product_{i=a+1}^{b} ((1 - q^(r+i)) / (1 - q^i)).

Evaluate at q^(-1). For each i,
(1 - q^(-(r+i))) / (1 - q^(-i)) = (-q^(-(r+i))(1 - q^(r+i))) / (-q^(-i)(1 - q^i)) = q^(-r) (1 - q^(r+i)) / (1 - q^i).
Multiplying these identities for i = a+1, ..., b gives
R_{a,b,r}(q^(-1)) = product_{i=a+1}^{b} q^(-r) (1 - q^(r+i)) / (1 - q^i)
= q^(-r(b-a)) product_{i=a+1}^{b} (1 - q^(r+i)) / (1 - q^i)
= q^(-D) R_{a,b,r}(q).
Multiplying by q^D yields the rational-function identity
q^D R_{a,b,r}(q^(-1)) = R_{a,b,r}(q)
in Z(q).

Now assume additionally that R_{a,b,r}(q) belongs to Z[q]. Since each factor 1 - q^m is a nonzero polynomial, the quotient defining R_{a,b,r}(q) is nonzero in Z(q); hence, when it lies in Z[q], it is a nonzero polynomial. Write
R_{a,b,r}(q) = sum_{j=0}^{m} d_j q^j
with d_m != 0 and each d_j in Z.
The self-reciprocity identity gives
sum_{j=0}^{m} d_j q^j = q^D R_{a,b,r}(q^(-1)) = sum_{j=0}^{m} d_j q^(D-j).
If some d_j with j > D were nonzero, then the right-hand side would contain the negative power q^(D-j). These exponents D-j are all distinct, so such a negative-power term could not cancel with any other term. But the left-hand side is an ordinary polynomial and has no negative powers. Therefore d_j = 0 for every j > D, so m <= D.

Now define integers c_0, ..., c_D by c_j = d_j for 0 <= j <= m and c_j = 0 for m < j <= D. Then
R_{a,b,r}(q) = sum_{j=0}^{D} c_j q^j.
Using again q^D R_{a,b,r}(q^(-1)) = R_{a,b,r}(q), we get
sum_{j=0}^{D} c_j q^j = q^D R_{a,b,r}(q^(-1)) = sum_{j=0}^{D} c_j q^(D-j) = sum_{j=0}^{D} c_{D-j} q^j,
where the last equality is the reindexing j -> D-j. Since equal polynomials have equal coefficients, c_j = c_{D-j} for every 0 <= j <= D.

This proves both the rational-function identity and the palindromic coefficient statement.

4. lem_20260329092547_6a64d34a: For integers a, b, r with 0 <= a <= b and r >= 0, let q be an indeterminate, define (q;q)_n := product_{j=1}^n (1 - q^j) for n >= 0 with (q;q)_0 := 1, set R_{a,b,r}(q) := ((q;q)_{r+b} (q;q)_a) / ((q;q)_{r+a} (q;q)_b), and define D := r (b - a). Assume that R_{a,b,r}(q) belongs to Z[q]. Then for every integer j with 0 <= j <= floor(D/2), the coefficient of q^j in R_{a,b,r}(q) is a nonnegative integer.
Let N := r+a+b. Since 0 <= a <= b and r >= 0, we have N >= b >= a >= 0; in particular 0 <= a <= N and 0 <= b <= N, and also N-a = r+b >= 0 and N-b = r+a >= 0. By the standard polynomial form of Gaussian q-binomial coefficients, for 0 <= t <= N one has [N choose t]_q = (q;q)_N / ((q;q)_t (q;q)_{N-t}). Therefore
[N choose b]_q / [N choose a]_q = ((q;q)_N / ((q;q)_b (q;q)_{N-b})) / ((q;q)_N / ((q;q)_a (q;q)_{N-a})) = ((q;q)_a (q;q)_{N-a}) / ((q;q)_b (q;q)_{N-b}).
Using N-a = r+b and N-b = r+a, this becomes
[N choose b]_q / [N choose a]_q = ((q;q)_{r+b} (q;q)_a) / ((q;q)_{r+a} (q;q)_b) = R_{a,b,r}(q).
Thus R_{a,b,r}(q) is exactly a quotient of two Gaussian q-binomial coefficients. By hypothesis R_{a,b,r}(q) belongs to Z[q], so this quotient is a polynomial in q. Applying the allowed semantic anchor with n = N, k = b, and l = a, we conclude that every coefficient of R_{a,b,r}(q) is nonnegative. Since R_{a,b,r}(q) is in Z[q], all of its coefficients are integers. Therefore, for every integer j with 0 <= j <= floor(D/2), the coefficient of q^j in R_{a,b,r}(q) is a nonnegative integer. This proves the lemma.

5. lem_20260329092603_a2bb7a49: Let D be a nonnegative integer, and let F(q) = sum_{j=0}^D c_j q^j be a polynomial in Z[q]. Assume that c_j = c_{D-j} for every integer j with 0 <= j <= D, and assume also that c_j >= 0 for every integer j with 0 <= j <= floor(D/2). Then c_j >= 0 for every integer j with 0 <= j <= D. Equivalently, every coefficient of F(q) is nonnegative.
Let j be any integer with 0 <= j <= D. We will prove that c_j >= 0.

If j <= floor(D/2), then c_j >= 0 by the given hypothesis on the first half of the coefficients.

Now suppose j > floor(D/2). We claim that D - j <= floor(D/2). Indeed, if D - j were also > floor(D/2), then, since j and D-j are integers, we would have j >= floor(D/2) + 1 and D - j >= floor(D/2) + 1. Adding these inequalities gives
D = j + (D-j) >= 2 floor(D/2) + 2.
But 2 floor(D/2) is either D or D-1, so 2 floor(D/2) + 2 > D, a contradiction. Therefore D-j <= floor(D/2). Also D-j >= 0 because j <= D.

Hence 0 <= D-j <= floor(D/2), so by the hypothesis on the first half of the coefficients we get c_{D-j} >= 0. Using the symmetry hypothesis, c_j = c_{D-j}, and therefore c_j >= 0.

Since j was arbitrary, we have proved that c_j >= 0 for every integer j with 0 <= j <= D. Equivalently, every coefficient of F(q) is nonnegative.
